reference.source: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours
clinicalPearls: A rare congenital or perinatal salivary neoplasm, arising most often in the parotid and less commonly the submandibular gland.
It presents at birth or in the neonatal period as a firm mass, and may be detected on antenatal imaging.
Histology recapitulates primitive salivary anlage, with basaloid epithelial cells in organoid nests showing peripheral palisading and both ductal and myoepithelial differentiation.
Behaviour is variable and best regarded as of low to intermediate malignant potential, with a real risk of local recurrence and occasional metastasis.
Recognised associations include hepatoblastoma, nevus sebaceus and other congenital anomalies, and molecular studies have identified HRAS, PIK3CA and beta-catenin alterations.
Complete surgical excision with facial nerve preservation where feasible is the mainstay of management.
Chemotherapy has a role for unresectable, incompletely excised or aggressive tumours.
It must be distinguished from other congenital head and neck masses such as teratoma, haemangioma and embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma.
reference.pathophysiology: Sialoblastoma is thought to arise from retained primitive (blastematous) salivary gland epithelium that fails to complete normal differentiation, producing a tumour that mirrors the embryonic developing gland. Neoplastic basaloid cells are organised into solid and organoid nests with peripheral palisading and focal ductal lumina, reflecting arrested dual epithelial and myoepithelial differentiation. Molecular studies have implicated activation of growth-signalling pathways, with reported HRAS and PIK3CA mutations and beta-catenin (WNT pathway) alterations driving proliferation of the primitive epithelium. The recognised association with hepatoblastoma and certain cutaneous and congenital anomalies suggests that, in some cases, sialoblastoma forms part of a broader developmental or embryonal tumour predisposition.
additionalDifferentials: Neuroblastoma or other small round blue cell tumour
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the head and neck to define extent and relation to the facial nerve
Biopsy with histology and immunohistochemistry for ductal and myoepithelial markers
Serum alpha-fetoprotein interpreted in the neonatal context, and to help exclude teratoma
Staging imaging where malignant behaviour is suspected
redFlags: Evidence of regional or distant metastasis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is variable; complete excision offers a good outcome, but local recurrence is not uncommon and close surveillance is required. Metastasis is infrequent but reported, and outcome is worse with incompletely excised or aggressive tumours.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for a benign basal cell adenoma and undertreating
Underestimating the risk of local recurrence after excision
Achieving incomplete excision, particularly around the facial nerve in a neonate
references: WHO Classification of Head and Neck Tumours
Gnepp's Diagnostic Surgical Pathology of the Head and Neck
Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
management: Complete surgical excision with preservation of the facial nerve where feasible as the mainstay of treatment
Adjuvant chemotherapy for incompletely resected, recurrent or metastatic tumours
MRI-based mapping of tumour extent and its relation to the facial nerve to guide resection
Histological and immunohistochemical confirmation with ductal and myoepithelial markers
Close post-operative surveillance for local recurrence given the low-to-intermediate malignant potential
Screening for associated hepatoblastoma with serum alpha-fetoprotein and imaging
Management within a multidisciplinary paediatric head-and-neck oncology team
